Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

reference notes:
The fictional Cedar Lane Volunteer Desk works out of two rooms at the Easton Library, with a folding table near the side entrance for evening drop-ins. Its volunteers answer requests for practical help, such as carrying groceries, finding a ride to an appointment, or getting a printed form. The desk began using a shared inbox last winter after several volunteers noticed that handwritten messages were difficult to pass between shifts. A laminated sign beside the inbox says, “If you leave a message, tell us how we can reach you.” The sign is a reminder for visitors, not a description of the code below.

On Mondays, Nia Brooks opens the inbox at 9:15 a.m. and checks whether a message includes a callback number. On Thursdays, Omar Patel often covers the first hour while Nia is at the library’s front desk. Volunteers mark messages as read only after one person has taken responsibility for following up. A blue paper folder holds messages that need a second look, while a green folder contains completed paper forms. The folders are part of the desk’s routine, and neither folder is represented in the supplied function.

The group’s April meeting took place in the smaller library room because a children’s reading circle had booked the main room. Six volunteers attended, and Sam Lee brought a printed list of questions that had come up during the previous month. “We should be able to say what the program actually checks,” Sam said, “without claiming it checks something just because our volunteers do.” The group agreed to keep their real-life intake notes separate from any discussion of the short function, so that the code review would not quietly turn into a description of the whole service.

During one Tuesday shift, a visitor called Mara left a message asking for help carrying two grocery bags up a flight of stairs. The inbox record had a callback number, but Mara did not say whether the request was urgent. A volunteer wrote the date on a paper slip and called her the following afternoon. That sequence describes a desk interaction, not a behavior established by the supplied code. In another case, a message from Eli asked for a ride to a clinic and said that he could not answer calls before noon. The volunteer who read it passed the callback detail to the next shift rather than changing the message’s urgency status.

At the April meeting, Nia described a separate message from a family asking where to find a school enrollment form. The message was tagged urgent by its sender, although the desk had not yet confirmed whether the request needed same-day attention. Omar said, “A label in a message is something we can see; it is not the same thing as a decision about what happens next.” The volunteers recorded the example because it showed why their notes use careful wording. No one at the meeting claimed that the code validates a sender, checks a phone number, or confirms the reason for an urgent label.

The shared inbox is a basic spreadsheet export with one row per message. In the export used for the meeting, the columns included a short description, a contact preference, an age field when it had been supplied, and a flag that volunteers entered when a sender described the matter as urgent. A blank age cell was exported as an absent value in some rows and as zero in others, depending on which volunteer had entered the row. The volunteers had not yet written a standard procedure for handling those differences. For the code discussion, the group planned to look only at the exact function provided below, not to infer how the spreadsheet export works.

1. In a practice session, four volunteers read sample inbox slips aloud and compared how each person described the urgency flag. They found that one person tended to call anything time-sensitive “urgent,” while another used that word only when the sender had explicitly said so. The group wrote down the disagreement but did not adopt a shared definition at that meeting. Their discussion is background about how the word appeared in volunteer conversations; it does not add conditions to the function.
2. A follow-up note from Sam recorded that some messages had no age information and that a missing value was not always entered in the same way. Sam asked the team to avoid treating a blank field as proof of a person’s age. The note did not specify a policy for missing ages, and the volunteers left that issue open for their next meeting.
3. Omar brought two anonymized examples to the room: one message marked urgent with an age value below thirteen, and another marked urgent with an age value above that number. He used them to ask which parts of a routing decision could be read directly from a short code sample. The examples were discussion prompts, not reports that the function had been run on those records.
4. The group copied the function into the meeting notes so that everyone would be looking at the same material. It is the complete supplied snippet:

def route_message(message):
    if message.get('urgent') and message.get('age', 0) < 13:
        return 'priority'
    return 'standard'

A later meeting was postponed when the library closed early for maintenance, so the volunteers did not settle their open questions about spreadsheet entry or the meaning of urgency. Nia put the April notes in the blue folder and added a reminder to bring them back to the next discussion. The volunteers still wanted a clear account of what could be concluded from the function itself, what could not be concluded from that code alone, and what example tests would be useful for examining its stated behavior. They asked that the code remain the sole basis for the explanation, review, and test suggestions, rather than treating the surrounding service notes as rules implemented by the function.
